ety: Shortened form of "of the clock", from Middle English of the clokke [from late 14th c.].

s.def: indication of time (the translations below are of "one o’clock")

In conjunction with a numeral, indicates the time within a twelve-hour period (midnight to noon or noon to midnight), specifically the time when the hour hand of a clock points precisely to the symbol or marking corresponding to the designated numeral, i.e., at the hour.
ex: We are expected to be there at six o'clock in the morning!
It is two o'clock.
What o'clock is it?

s.def: Used to indicate that it is time to do a specific action, or time for a specific action to occur.
ex: I'm feeling peckish; I think it must be nearly dinner o'clock.
We're here at Waffle House, and it's waffles o'clock!
Hooray! Beer o'clock!

s.def: A place or situation of fruitfulness or abundance separated from surrounding barrenness or scarcity.

Why should I not speak to him or to any human being who walks upright upon this oblate orange?
’Tis prolate, still,’ with a long dejected Geordie O. ‘Isn’t it…?’ ‘I’m an Astronomer,– trust me, ’tis gone well to oblate.’

s.def: To offer as either a gift or an oblation.

ety: From Middle English oblacioun, from Old French oblacion, from Latin oblātiō (“offering”), from offerō (“to offer, present”). By surface analysis, oblate + -ion.

s.def: The offering of worship, thanks etc. to a deity.
ex: whatever she judged proper for the oblation of the approaching night.
As she waits for her children in the shade / Demogorgon or demigod the ghost parade / No oblation will bring her back to our place

s.def: A deed or gift offered charitably.

ety: First attested in 1533; borrowed from Latin obligātus, perfect passive participle of obligō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of oblige, taken through French.

s.def: To bind, compel, constrain, or oblige by a social, legal, or moral tie.
To cause to be grateful or indebted; to oblige.
To commit (money, for example) in order to fulfill an obligation.
Requiring a (specified) way of life, habitat, etc.
ex: [A]nalysis of the chemical composition of their bones reveals that they were obligate carnivores.

s.def: Indispensable; essential; necessary; obligatory; mandatory; unavoidably invoked.
ex: In addition to being the obligate food source for monarch caterpillars, milkweeds also provide abundant nectar for the adult butterflies.
In some languages such signaling is optional, whereas in others it is obligate.
Unlike for phagotrophic flagellates, bacteria serve as a facultative rather than an obligate food source for crustacean zooplankton.

s.def: Bound by oath, law or duty.
An obligate organism.

ety: From Middle English obligacioun, from Old French obligacion, from Latin obligatio, obligationem, from obligatum (past participle of obligare), from ob- (“to”) + ligare (“to bind”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵ- (“to bind”).

s.def: The act of binding oneself by a social, legal, or moral tie to someone.
A social, legal, or moral requirement, duty, contract, or promise that compels someone to follow or avoid a particular course of action.
ex: I feel I'm under obligation to attend my sister's wedding, even though we have a very frosty relationship.

s.def: A course of action imposed by society, law, or conscience by which someone is bound or restricted.
A legal agreement stipulating a specified action or forbearance by a party to the agreement; the document containing such agreement.
Reason for being obliged to, that is, grateful for, something.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁óp(i) Proto-Italic *op Latin ob Latin ob- Proto-Indo-European *leyǵ-der. Middle English obligatorie English obligatory From Middle English obligatorie, from Latin obligatōrius.

s.def: Imposing obligation, legally, morally, or otherwise; binding; mandatory.
ex: an obligatory promise

s.def: Requiring a matter or obligation.

ety: From Middle English obligen, from Old French obligier, obliger, from Latin obligō, obligāre, from ob- + ligō. Doublet of obligate, taken straight from Latin.

s.def: To cause somebody to feel indebted.
ex: I am much obliged to you for your recent help.

s.def: To constrain someone by force or by social, moral or legal means.
ex: Your carelessness obliges firmness on my part.
I am obliged to report to the police station every week.

s.def: To do (someone) a service or favour (hence, originally, creating an obligation).
ex: He obliged me by not parking his car in the drive.
The singer obliged(us) with an encore.

s.def: Happy and ready to do favours for others.
present participle and gerund of oblige
The imposition of an obligation.
ex: Many were the finings, and excommunications, and the obligings to do penances, that took place at this time.

ety: From oblige + -or.

s.def: The party bearing a legal obligation to another party (the obligee).

ety: From Middle French oblique, from Latin oblīquus (also spelled oblīcus) (“slanting, sideways, indirect, envious”).

s.def: Not erect or perpendicular; not parallel to, or at right angles from, the base.
ex: Italic fonts are sometimes described as oblique in typographic terminology.
when it has a Direction oblique to that of the former Motion, it is either added to, or subtracted from the former Motion

s.def: Not straightforward; indirect; by implication; (sometimes even) obscure, ambiguous, or confusing.
ex: The email from HR obliquely informed her that some complaints about her had been received.
This mode of oblique research, where a more direct one is denied, we find to be the only one in our power.

s.def: Disingenuous; underhand; morally corrupt.
ex: Then would be closed the restless, oblique eye / That looks for evil, like a treacherous spy

s.def: Not direct in descent; not following the line of father and son; collateral.
ex: His natural affection in a direct line was strong; in an oblique, but weak; for no man ever loved Children more, or a Brother less.

s.def: Having the base of the blade asymmetrical, with one side lower than the other.
Growing at an angle that is neither vertical nor horizontal.
ex: Oblique and sinker roots will normally be under a greater compression stress than lateral roots.

s.def: Pertaining to the oblique case (non-nominative).

Indirect; employing the actual words of the speaker but as related by a third person, having the first person in pronoun and verb converted into the third person and adverbs of present time into the past, etc.
ex: They found out obliquely that she had heard from HR about the comments and was taking some time to absorb the sting of an implied reprimand.

s.def: Employing oblique motion, motion or progression in which one part (voice) stays on the same note while another ascends or descends.
ex: In passing from the minor third to unison, the motion ought to be oblique, but from the major third to unison the motion ought to be similar

s.def: An oblique line.

ety: PIE word *h₁epi (start of 17th century) From earlier obliterat, learned borrowing from Latin obliterātus, oblitterātus (“having been blotted out, effaced, erased; having been forgotten”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix, of participial origin)). Obliterātus and oblitterātus are respectively the perfect passive participles of obliterō and oblitterō (“to blot out, efface, erase, obliterate; to cause to be forgotten”), probably either: * from ob- (prefix meaning ‘against; towards’) + littera (“lette…

s.def: To destroy (someone or something) completely, leaving no trace; to annihilate, to wipe out.
ex: Soham's station had been completely obliterated (the replacement was to close in 1965 and is only now being reopened).
The initial damage assessment suggests that President Trump’s claim that Iran’s nuclear facilities were “obliterated” was overstated.

s.def: To hide (something) by covering it; to conceal, to obscure.
ex: The rainclouds obliterated the sun as they swept across the sky.

s.def: To make (a drawing, text which is printed or written, etc.) indecipherable, either by erasing or obscuring it; to blot out, to efface, to delete.
ex: The walls had been rudely painted, (for arras then was rare, even among the wealthiest,) but the colours were half obliterated by time and damp.
At least she could not be comfortable there till long years should have obliterated her keen consciousness of it.

s.def: To impair the function and/or structure of (a body cavity, vessel, etc.) by ablating or occluding it (in the latter case, chiefly by filling it with tissue).
ex: The pleural sac was obliterated by firm fibrous adhesions over the right upper lobe.

s.def: To cancel (a postage stamp) with a postmark so it cannot be reused.
To be destroyed completely, leaving no trace.
Of a body cavity, vessel, etc.: to close up or fill with tissue; of perfusion or a pulse: to cease owing to obstruction.
ex: distal pulses obliterate until perfusion is restored

s.def: Of markings on an insect: difficult to distinguish from the background; faint, indistinct.
Completely destroyed or erased; effaced, obliterated.
ex: […] then how swiftly and how wonderfully, he reads all the obscurest and most obliterate inscriptions he finds in his memory; […]

ety: Inherited from Middle English oblivion, from Anglo-Norman oblivion, from Latin oblīviō (“forgetfulness”), from oblīvīscor (“to forget”).

s.def: The state of being completely forgotten, of being reduced to a state of non-existence, extinction, or nothingness, including through war and destruction. (Figuratively) for an area like hell, a wasteland.
ex: They tried to bomb them into oblivion.
I will cast them into oblivion!
Ordo Malleus Inquisitor: I hereby sign the death warrant of an entire world, and consign a million souls to oblivion.

s.def: state of forgetfulness or distraction
The state of forgetting completely, of being oblivious, unconscious, unaware, as when sleeping, drunk, or dead.
ex: He regularly drank himself into oblivion.
Only the oblivion of sleep can heal the greatest traumas.

s.def: A form of purgatory.
Amnesty.
To consign to oblivion; to efface utterly.

ety: From Middle English oblivious, from Latin oblīviōsus (“forgetful, oblivious”), formed from oblīvium (“forgetfulness, oblivion”) + -ōsus (“full of, overly, prone to”), from oblīvīscor (“to forget”).

s.def: Lacking awareness; unmindful; unaware, unconscious of.
ex: Your grandmother is completely oblivious to her surroundings.

s.def: Forgetful.
ex: He's hopelessly oblivious, always forgetting his appointments.

ety: From Middle English oblong, oblonge, borrowed from Latin oblongus.

s.def: Having a length and width that are different; not square or circular.
ex: The room was quite dark. The oblong window showed the night sky pricked here and there with stars.

s.def: Roughly rectangular or elliptical.
ex: Plant upright spreading hardy, vigorous and productive; berry, oblong, round, medium size, sweet but rather ideipid.

s.def: Having the horizontal axis of a page longer than the vertical; In landscape orientation.
ex: Of the smaller oblong formats, none is specifically designated for music.
Mass cycles and motets had never been presented in small oblong format, so far as we can tell.

s.def: Something with an oblong shape.
A rectangle with length and width that are different.
An ellipse with minor and major axes that are different.
To extend so as to form an oblong shape.
To give an oblong shape to.
ex: A. Why, by dropping them off of cars or dropping them off of trucks or some way it would oblong them .
His silhouette: broad shoulders, big legs, a square face oblonged by a crest of thick hair and almost lantern jaw.
And there were suddenly berries where there had been none before, bright red and bright blue, all with a careless water drop oblonging their form.

ety: From Middle English obloqui, obloquie, obloquy, from Middle French obloquie and its etymon Late Latin obloquium (“contradiction”), from Latin obloquor (“speak against, contradict”). By surface analysis, ob- + -loquy.

s.def: Abusive language.
ex: The Territory suffered in consequence, and once more a storm of obloquy was cast upon her.
“Can't you understand that love without confidence is a worthless thing—and that had you trusted me I would have borne any obloquy with you.[…]”

s.def: Disgrace.
ex: Her death I could have born, but the death of her honour has added obloquy and shame to that sorrow which bends my grey hairs to the dust!
His name undoubtedly stands very high in the present age, and will in all probability go down to posterity with more or less of renown or obloquy.

s.def: A false accusation; malevolent rumors.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁óp(i) Proto-Italic *op Latin ob Latin ob- Proto-Indo-European *neḱ-der. s.def: Extremely offensive or unpleasant; very annoying, contemptible, or odious.
ex: Throwing stones at the bus is another example of your obnoxious behaviour.
The disturbance had commenced, like those of England, in the refusal of the parliament to sanction an obnoxious tax; but here all resemblance ended.
For my part, thumb-marks [in books] I find very obnoxious—far more so than the spoiling of the binding.

s.def: Unjustly disagreeable, argumentative or objectionable; brazenly rude.
ex: He was an especially obnoxious and detestable specimen of a man.
I always feel out of place when I am around people. I feel obnoxious if I laugh or talk too much.

s.def: Exposed or vulnerable to something, especially harm or injury.
ex: It is our comfort, while we are obnoxious to so many accidents, that we are under the care of One who directs contingencies, […]

s.def: Causing harm or injury; harmful, hurtful, injurious.
Deserving of blame or punishment; blameworthy, guilty.
Under the authority or power of someone; subject, subordinate; hence, deferential, submissive, subservient.
Followed by to: likely to do something.

ety: An earlier form in English is hautboy, but the spelling oboe was adopted into English ca. 1770 from the Italian oboè, a transliteration in that language's orthography of the 17th-century pronunciation of the French word hautbois, a compound word made of haut (“high, loud, high-pitched”) and bois (“wood, woodwind”).

s.def: A soprano and melody wind instrument in the modern orchestra and wind ensemble. It is a smaller instrument and generally made of grenadilla wood. It is a member of the double reed family.
ex: Whistles, mirlitons, flutes, trumpets or horns, clarinets, and oboes are all played in one or more parts of the continent.

s.def: Someone who plays an oboe.

ety: From ob- (“inverse”) + ovate (“egg-shaped”).

s.def: Shaped like an egg, with the broad extremity located away from the base.
Abbreviation of obsolete.
Clipping of observed.
Police observation.

Had you under obs for three weeks.

s.def: An observation hut.

ety: From Middle French obscene (modern French obscène (“indecent, obscene”)), and from its etymon Latin obscēnus, obscaenus (“inauspicious; ominous; disgusting, filthy; offensive, repulsive; indecent, lewd, obscene”). The further etymology is uncertain, but may be from ob- (prefix meaning ‘towards’) + caenum (“dirt, filth; mire, mud”) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweyn- (“to make dirty, soil; filth; mud”)) or scaevus (“left, on the left side; clumsy; (figurative) unlucky”) (from P…

s.def: Offensive to standards of decency or morality.
ex: What is obscene today may not be so tomorrow or what is obscene at one place may not be obscene at another place.

s.def: Lewd or lustful.
ex: All masturbation is obscene, for [Roger] Scruton, also because it "involves a concentration on the body and its curious pleasures" [...].
He [Justin Martyr] asks how pagan gods who exhibit the same destructive passions and obscene desires as wicked humans can be worthy of worship.

s.def: Disgusting or repulsive.
ex: The reminder of who we were / made the canned laughter obscene. / Disgusted, mother returned to the kitchen, / her thoughts private.
Her mom made her break up with me when she found a note I wrote to Linda; she found it obscene. I found HER obscene.

s.def: Beyond all reason; excessive.
ex: "You ate an obscene amount of those lobster patties last night, Deb." / "And I plan to eat an obscene amount of them tonight as well," I replied.
She would probably jump at the chance to show everyone how to save an obscene amount of money with an obscene amount of coupons.

s.def: Liable to corrupt or deprave.
To act or speak in an obscene manner; to offend.

ety: From obscene + -ity, from Latin obscenitas.

s.def: Lewdness, indecency, or offensive behaviour or material.
ex: The coalition of religious conservatives was campaigning against, in their view, rampant obscenity in the entertainment industry.

s.def: Something that is obscene.
ex: Martha wouldn't go into the art museum because, as she put it, "They have obscenities just sitting out, on display!"

s.def: An act of obscene behaviour.
ex: Bestiality was outlawed as an obscenity in the strongly conservative community.

s.def: Specifically, an offensive word; a profanity; a dirty word.
ex: Eliza couldn't stand her daughter's music; as she saw it, it was just shouted obscenities and a heavy drum beat.

s.def: The fact of being obscene.

ety: Entering English circa 1793–1799: From German Obskurant and French obscurant, from classical Latin obscūrant-, stem of obscūrāns, present participle of obscūrāre (“to obscure”), from obscūrus (“dark”).

s.def: Acting or tending to confound, obfuscate, or obscure.
Typical of or pertaining to obscurants; obscurantic; obscurantistic.
One who acts to confound or obfuscate; an obscurantist.
A person who seeks to prevent or hinder enquiry and the advancement of knowledge or wisdom; an agent of endarkenment.
An opposer of lucidity and transparency in the political and intellectual spheres.

ety: From Latin obscūrātiō. By surface analysis, obscure + -ation.

s.def: The state of being obscured.
A unit of measurement used in particular for smoke detectors which respond to absorption of light by smoke, in percent absorption per unit length, e.g. % obs/ft, % obs/m.

ety: From Middle English obscure, from Old French obscur, from Latin obscūrus (“dark, dusky, indistinct”), from ob- + *scūrus, from Proto-Italic *skoiros, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱeh₃-. Doublet of oscuro.

s.def: Dark, faint or indistinct.
ex: I found myself in an obscure wood.
His lamp shall be put out in obscure darkness.

s.def: Hidden, out of sight or inconspicuous.
ex: The obscure bird / Clamoured the livelong night.
the obscure corners of the earth

s.def: Difficult to understand; abstruse.
ex: an obscure passage or inscription; The speaker made obscure references to little-known literary works.
The lock was of a kind that Watt could not pick. Watt could pick simple locks, but he could not pick obscure locks.

s.def: Not well-known.
ex: i need to be REALLY careful to not use any obscure words. otherwise my tweets might end up on a wiktionary page

s.def: Unknown or uncertain; unclear.
ex: The etymological roots of the word "blizzard" are obscure and open to debate.

s.def: To render obscure; to darken; to make dim; to keep in the dark; to hide; to make less visible, intelligible, legible, glorious, beautiful, or illustrious.
ex: They are all couched in a pit hard by Herne's oak, with obscured lights.
c. 1688', William Wake, Preparation for Death There is scarce any duty which has been so obscured in the writings of learned men as this.

s.def: To hide, put out of sight etc.
ex: It has been little altered over the years save for the addition of a platform awning which rather obscures the arcaded entrance to the booking hall.
I realized that the purpose of writing is to inflate weak ideas, obscure poor reasoning, and inhibit clarity.

s.def: To conceal oneself; to hide.
ex: How! There's bad news. / I must obscure, and hear it.

ety: Plural of obsequy; from Middle English obsequias, obsequies, obsequyes, from Latin obsequiae.

s.def: Funeral rites.
plural of obsequy.
plural of obsequie.

ety: From Middle English obsequyous, from Latin obsequiōsus (“complaisant, obsequious”), from obsequium (“compliance”), from obsequor (“comply with, yield to”), from ob (“in the direction of, towards”) + sequor (“follow”) (cf. sequel).

s.def: Excessively eager and attentive to please or to obey instructions; fawning, subservient, servile.
ex: [S]he complained pettishly of the heat and the flies and at length of the walk, and reduced Robert to the antics of an obsequious dog.

s.def: Obedient; compliant with someone else's orders or wishes.
Of or pertaining to obsequies, funereal.

ety: Etymology tree English observe Proto-Indo-European *-dʰlom Proto-Italic *-ðlom Proto-Italic *-ðlis Latin -bilis Latin -ābilis Old French -ablebor. Middle English -able English -able English observable From observe + -able.

s.def: Able to be observed.
ex: The strange new star was at the edge of the observable universe.

s.def: Deserving to be observed; worth regarding; remarkable.
Any physical property that can be observed and measured directly and not derived from other properties.
ex: Temperature is an observable but entropy is derived.

s.def: The extent of a universe within the cosmological horizon of an observer.

ety: From Old French observance, from Latin observantia. Equivalent of observe + -ance.

s.def: The practice of complying with a law, custom, command or rule.
The custom of celebrating a holiday or similar occasion.
Observation or the act of watching.
A rule governing a religious order, especially in the Roman Catholic church.
ex: Thomas Merton was a monk in the Order of Cistertians of the Strict Observance.

s.def: That which is to be observed.
Reverence; homage.

ety: Borrowed from French observant.

s.def: Alert and paying close attention; watchful.
ex: The observant police officer noticed that my tax disk was out-of-date.

s.def: Diligently attentive in observing a law, custom, duty or principle; regardful; mindful.
ex: I was normally observant of the local parking restrictions.
We are told how observant Alexander was of his master Aristotle.

s.def: Practicing a religion.
ex: She is an observant Catholic who goes to church regularly.

ety: From Middle English observacion, borrowed from Middle French observacion. Also a borrowing from French observation and a learned borrowing from Latin observātiō(n-). Morphologically observe + -ation.

s.def: The act of observing, and the fact of being observed (see observance)
The act of noting and recording some event; or the record of such noting.
A remark or comment.
ex: That's a foolish observation.
To observations which ourselves we make / We grow more partial for the observer's sake.

s.def: A judgement based on observing.
An evaluation conducted through observing.
ex: I need to do your observation before the end of the week.

s.def: Performance of what is prescribed; adherence in practice; observance.
ex: We are to procure dispensation or leave to omit the observation of it in such circumstances.

s.def: A regime under which a subject is routinely observed.
A realization of a random variable.
a lookout or vantage point

ety: Borrowed from French observatoire, equivalent to observe + -atory.

s.def: A place where stars, planets and other celestial bodies are observed, usually through a telescope; also place for observing meteorological or other natural phenomena.
ex: The corporation of Harvard University have passed a vote closing the observatory in Cambridge to the public on Saturday evenings.
At the observatory on Mauna Kea on Hawaii, a young astronomer, Heidi Hammel, focuses a huge telescope on the remote planet.

s.def: A lookout (vantage point with a view of the surrounding area)

ety: From Middle French observer, from Old French observer, from Latin observō (“to watch”), from ob- (“before”) + servō (“to keep”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to guard”). Cognate with Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐍂𐍅𐌰 (sarwa, “weapons, armour”), Old English searu (“device”).

s.def: To notice or view, especially carefully or with attention to detail.
ex: From this vantage point we can observe the behavior of the animals in their natural habitat.
She got up before dawn to observe the lunar eclipse.
“One horse?” interjected Holmes. ¶ “Yes, only one.” ¶ “Did you observe the colour?”

s.def: To follow or obey the custom, practice, or rules (especially of a religion).
ex: Please observe all posted speed limits.

s.def: To take note of and celebrate (a holiday or similar occurrence), to keep; to follow (a type of time or calendar reckoning).
ex: Ye shall observe the feast of unleavened bread.
On Sunday, most of Canada will observe daylight time and spring forward an hour in order to reflect the increasing sunlight.

s.def: To comment on something; to make an observation.
ex: The senator observed that the bill would be detrimental to his constituents.

s.def: An observation (remark, comment or judgement).

ety: Etymology tree English observe Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English observer From observe + -er.

s.def: One who makes observations, monitors or takes notice.
ex: Most impartial observers agreed that Sampras had not served well.

s.def: One who adheres or follows laws, guidelines, etc.
ex: I shall be an observer of the local customs.

s.def: A person sent as a representative, to a meeting or other function to monitor but not to participate.
ex: The UN sent many observers to the country's first elections.
When the army reached Tsun-i, an enlarged Politburo meeting was called. Teng attended as an observer.

s.def: A country or other entity which has limited participation rights within an organization.
ex: The Vatican and Palestine have observer status at the UN.

s.def: A crew member on an aircraft who makes observations of enemy positions or aircraft.
ex: The only crew-member to survive the crash was the Canadian observer.

s.def: A sentry etc. manning an observation post.
ex: We waited till dusk when the observers' vision was poorest.

s.def: Synonym of spotter.

ety: From Latin obsessus, perfect passive participle of obsideō (“sit on or in, remain, besiege”), from ob- (“before”) + sedeō (“to sit”); see sit, session, etc.; compare assess, possess.

s.def: To be preoccupied with a single topic or emotion.
ex: Some people are obsessed with sports.

s.def: To dominate the thoughts of someone.
ex: Thoughts of her obsess my every waking moment.

s.def: To think or talk obsessively about.
ex: Stop obsessing over it, will you!

s.def: Intensely preoccupied with or by a given topic or emotion; driven by a specified obsession.
Influenced or controlled by evil spirits, but less than possessed in that the spirits do not actually reside in the victim.
ex: What of demon possession, whereby a person is not only obsessed or oppressed by evil spirits, but these spirits actually reside in such a person?

ety: From Latin obsessio (“a besieging”), from obsidere (“to besiege”); see obsess. Equivalent to obsess + -ion.

s.def: An activity or entity that inspires a compulsive and potentially unhealthy fixation, or the fixation thereby inspired.
ex: Editing Wikipedia started as a hobby, but it's turned into a complete obsession of mine.
His current obsession is getting that law passed.

s.def: An idea that engenders a compulsive or irrational preoccupation, or the preoccupation thereby engendered.
ex: The downfall of the chairman is an obsession that consumes Laura's time.

s.def: Influence or control by evil spirits without possession.
The quality of being obsessed; an unshakeable feeling that one topic or activity must be pursued above other interests.
ex: My obsession with rugby resulted in me spending years following the sport.

ety: Etymology tree English obsess Proto-Indo-European *-wós Proto-Indo-European *-iHwósder. Latin -īvus Old French -ifbor. Middle English -yf English -ive English obsessive From obsess + -ive.

s.def: Having one thought or pursuing one activity (an obsession) to the absolute or nearly absolute exclusion of all others.
ex: Hardcore fans' obsessive behavior may take over their lives.

s.def: Prone to cause obsession.
ex: The idea is too tempting, it's obsessive.

s.def: Excessive, as results from obsession.
ex: A workaholic's obsessive zeal may lead to success or burnout.

s.def: A person who is obsessed, who has an obsession.

ety: From Latin obsidianus; named after Obsidius, who was, according to Pliny, the Roman who discovered the stone in Aethiopia.

s.def: A type of naturally occurring black glass produced by volcanoes.
A slightly bluish black, the color of obsidian glass.

ety: From Middle English obsidional, from Latin obsidiōnālis, from obsidiō (“siege, blockade”), from obsidēre (“beset, besiege, hem in”).

s.def: Pertaining to a siege.

ety: From Latin obsolēscēns.

s.def: In the process of becoming obsolete, but not obsolete yet.
ex: How can I live among this gentle obsolescent breed of heroes, and not weep?

s.def: No longer in use or no longer useful; now disused or neglected (often in favour of something newer, better, or more fashionable); outmoded.
ex: Speedy, worldwide, accessible delivery of news through the Web has made newspapers obsolete.
Horses became obsolete means of transportation in cities in the first half of the twentieth century.

s.def: Imperfectly developed; not very distinct.
To cause to become obsolete.
ex: This software component has been obsoleted.
We are in the process of obsoleting this product.
Should we develop nonhuman minds that might eventually outnumber, outsmart, obsolete and replace us?

s.def: An obsolete thing or person.

ety: From Middle English obstacle, from Old French obstacle, from Latin obstāculum.

s.def: Something that impedes, stands in the way of, or holds up progress, either physically or figuratively
ex: A big obstacle to understanding the manual was that it had been poorly translated from the Japanese.

ety: From obstetrics + -ician.

s.def: A physician who specializes in childbirth.

ety: From obstetric.

s.def: The care of women during and after pregnancy.

ety: From obstinate + -cy.

s.def: The state, or an act, of stubbornness or doggedness.
ex: He finished only through a mixture of determined obstinacy and ingenuity.

ex: 🔥 An obstinacy of Bison stampeding down a road

ety: Inherited from Middle English obstinat(e) (“obstinate, stubborn”), from Latin obstinātus, perfect passive participle of obstinō (“set one's mind firmly upon, resolve”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ob (“before”) + *stinare, from stare (“to stand”). Doublet of ostinato.

ex: an obstinate blockage in the pipe

s.def: Of a facial feature or expression, fixed and unmoving.
ex: He had the same pile of curly hair, but he was clean-shaven with a heavy, obstinate jowl.

ex: My dress was draggled, my hat had slipped back, and the kinks and curls of my obstreperous hair were something awful.

ety: From Latin past participle stem obstruct- (“blocked up”), from verb obstruere, from ob (“against”) + struere (“pile up, build”).

s.def: To block or fill (a passage) with obstacles or an obstacle.
To impede, retard, or interfere with; hinder.
ex: They obstructed my progress.

s.def: To get in the way of so as to hide from sight.

ety: From Latin obstructio (“hindrance”), from obstruo (“build against, block, stop”).

s.def: The act of obstructing, or state of being obstructed.
Something which obstructs or impedes, either intentionally or unintentionally
ex: The referee stopped play because of an obstruction by the defender.

s.def: The condition of having the natural powers obstructed in their usual course; the arrest of the vital functions; death.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin obstruēns, obstruentis.

s.def: Causing obstruction; blocking up.
ex: an obstruent medicine

s.def: A consonant sound formed by obstructing the airway, causing turbulence; a plosive, fricative, or affricate.
Anything that obstructs, especially in the passages of the body.

ety: From Middle English obteinen, from Anglo-Norman obtenir, optiner et al., and Middle French obtenir, from Latin obtinēre (“to gain, achieve, succeed, possess”), from ob- + tenēre (“to hold”).

s.def: To get hold of; to gain possession of, to procure; to acquire, in any way.
ex: obtain permission
obtain information
difficult to obtain

s.def: To secure (that) a specific objective or state of affairs be reached.
To prevail, be victorious; to succeed.
ex: “O daughter deare!” (said she) “despeire no whit; / For never sore but might a salve obtain [...].”
This, though it failed at present, yet afterward obtained, and was a mighty step to the ruin of the commonwealth.

ety: From Latin obtrūdō (“thrust off or against”), from ob- (“ob-”) + trūdō (“thrust”).

s.def: To proffer (something) by force; to impose (something) on someone or into some area.
ex: By which we may see, that they who are not called to Counsell, can have no good Counsell in such cases to obtrude.

s.def: To become apparent in an unwelcome way, to be forcibly imposed; to jut in, to intrude (on or into).
ex: How you can bear such recollections, is astonishing to me!—They will sometimes obtrude—but how you can court them!
Sometimes I dreamed strangely of disturbed earth, and of hair, still golden and living, obtruded through the coffin-chinks.
Occasionally the thought obtruded itself that possibly at some later day Tarzan would regret his magnanimity, and claim his rights.

s.def: To impose (oneself) on others; to cut in.
ex: As 1968 began to ebb into 1969, however, and as “anticlimax” began to become a real word in my lexicon, another term began to obtrude itself.

ety: From Middle English obtuse, from Latin obtūsus (“blunt, dull; obtuse”), past participle of obtundere, from obtundō (“to batter, beat, strike; to blunt, dull”), from ob- (“against”) (see ob-) + tundō (“to beat, strike; to bruise, crush, pound”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewd-, from *(s)tew- (“to hit; to push”)). ex: Yet you do not brighten what would otherwise be dull, impart a keenness to the obtusest point, and diffuse a general lustre?

s.def: Intellectually dull or dim-witted.
Of sound, etc.: deadened, muffled, muted.
Indirect or circuitous.
To dull or reduce an emotion or a physical state.

ety: From Latin obversus, 1650s.

s.def: Turned or facing toward the observer.
ex: The obverse side of the gravestone has the inscription.

s.def: Corresponding; complementary.
ex: When you speak clearly, people understand you. If you don't mumble, the obverse effect is observed.

s.def: Having the base, or end next to the attachment, narrower than the top.
ex: an obverse leaf

s.def: The heads side of a coin, or the side of a medal or badge that has the principal design.
ex: The medal had a cross on the obverse and had a name inscribed on the reverse.

s.def: A proposition obtained by obversion.

ety: Latin obversio (“a turning towards”).

s.def: The act of turning toward or downward.
An immediate inference that denies the opposite of something previously affirmed.
ex: All men are mortal, so, by obversion, no men are immortal.

s.def: To turn so as to show another side.
To turn towards the front.
To infer by obversion; too convert a proposition to its obverse.
The result of obversion.

ety: First attested in 1567; borrowed from Latin obviātus, perfect passive participle of obviō (“to block, to hinder”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

s.def: To anticipate and prevent or bypass (something which would otherwise have been necessary or required); to render (something) unnecessary.
To avoid (a future problem or difficult situation).
ex: A mild dose of a warm active aperient to obviate costiveness, or to produce two motions daily, is generally very beneficial.

Thus, to obviate resistance, the discussion should be relevant to the patient′s problems.

s.def: Synonym of obviative.
Synonym of obviative.

ety: 16th century, from Latin obvius (“being in the way so as to meet, meeting, easy to access, at hand, ready, obvious”) + -ous, from ob- (“before”) + via (“way”).

s.def: Easily discovered, seen, or understood; self-explanatory.

ety: Named after the English Franciscan theologist William of Occam, an advocate of the law of parsimony, and the idea of a razor as a tool that trims or shaves.

ety: From Middle English occasioun, from Middle French occasion, from Old French occasiun, from Latin occāsiōnem, noun of action from perfect passive participle occāsus, from verb occidō, from prefix ob- (“down", "away”) + verb cadō (“fall”).

s.def: A person who does something only occasionally.

ety: From Middle English occasionally, occasionaly, occasyoneely, occasyonly, equivalent to occasional + -ly.

s.def: On an occasion, accidentally, by chance.
ex: Mr Tourville occasionally told his age; just turned of thirty-one.
I had met Lord Ossory in the forenoon, who had come to town occasionally.

s.def: On the occasion of something else happening; incidentally, by the way.

Being or relating to a kind of tube socket base having eight pins.

ety: From oct- + angle.

s.def: A geometric figure with eight corners, an octagon.

ety: From octa- + nitro- + cubane.

s.def: A high explosive derived from cubane, and one of the most powerful chemical explosives known.

ety: From Latin octāns. Doublet of Octans.

s.def: An instrument for measuring angles, particularly of elevation.
The eighth part of a circle; an arc of 45 degrees.
The aspect of two planets that are 45°, or one-eighth of a circle, apart.
The eighth part of a disc; a sector of 45 degrees; half a quadrant; one of eight divisions of a sphere by three orthogonal planes.

ety: From Latin octavus (“eighth”). Doublet of octavo, ochava, and oitava.

s.def: An interval of twelve semitones spanning eight degrees of the diatonic scale, representing a doubling or halving in pitch frequency.
ex: The melody jumps up an octave at the beginning, then later drops back down an octave.
The singer was known for astounding clarity over her entire five-octave range.
The octave has a pitch ratio of 2:1.

s.def: The pitch an octave higher than a given pitch.
ex: The bass starts on a low E, and the tenor comes in on the octave.

s.def: A coupler on an organ which allows the organist to sound the note an octave above the note of the key pressed (cf sub-octave)
A poetic stanza consisting of eight lines; usually used as one part of a sonnet.
ex: With mournful melody it continued this octave.

s.def: The eighth defensive position, with the sword hand held at waist height, and the tip of the sword out straight at knee level.
ex: If they always do a lateral parry quarte, and never a semicircular octave, that gives you an opening.

s.def: The day that is one week after a feast day in the Latin rite of the Catholic Church.
An eight-day period beginning on a feast day in the Latin rite of the Catholic Church.
A small cask of wine, one eighth of a pipe.
An octonion.
Any of a number of coherent-noise functions of differing frequency that are added together to form Perlin noise.

ety: From Latin octavo. Doublet of octave, oitava, and ochava.

s.def: A sheet of paper 7 to 10 inches (= 17.78 to 25.4 cm) high and 4.5 to 6 inches (= 11.43 to 15.24 cm) wide, the size varying with the large original sheet used to create it. It is made by folding the original sheet three times to produce eight leaves.
A book of octavo pages.

ety: From oct- + -ennial.

s.def: Occurring every eight years.
Lasting or taking eight years.

ety: From French octillion. By surface analysis, oct- (“eight”) + -illion.

s.def: A thousand trillion trillion, a billion billion billion: 1 followed by 27 zeros, 10²⁷.
ex: Altogether it takes seven billion billion billion (that’s 7,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000, or seven octillion) atoms to make you.

s.def: A trillion quintillion: 1 followed by 48 zeros, 10⁴⁸.

ety: Clipping of octopus

s.def: An octopus (safety device).

ety: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French octobre, from Latin Octōber (“eighth month”), from Latin octō (“eight”), from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw (“twice four”); + Latin -ber, from -bris, an adjectival suffix; October was the eighth month in the Roman calendar.

s.def: The tenth month of the Gregorian calendar, following September and preceding November.
ex: Holonyms: calendar year; year
By October it was advancing steadily toward Pangwa, encountering meager resistance.

s.def: A female given name transferred from the month name.

ety: From Latin octōgēnārius + -an (suffix forming adjectives and representative nouns), either directly or via French octogénaire, from Latin octōgēnus (“80 each”) + -ārius (“-ary”), from octōgintā (“eight tens, 80”).

s.def: Synonym of eightysomething: a person between 80 and 89 years old.
ex: Finsbury Park station, one of the most important L.N.E.R. suburban junctions, is now an octogenarian.

s.def: Of or related to eightysomethings.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw Proto-Hellenic *oktṓ Ancient Greek ὀκτώ (oktṓ) Proto-Indo-European *ped- Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *pṓdsder. Ancient Greek πούς (poús) Ancient Greek ὀκτώπους (oktṓpous)bor. Latin octōpūsbor. English octopus Borrowed from Latin octōpūs, from Ancient Greek ὀκτώπους (oktṓpous), from ὀκτώ (oktṓ, “eight”) + πούς (poús, “foot”). Piecewise doublet of octopod and octopede.

s.def: A mollusc from genus Octopus.
Any of several marine molluscs of the order Octopoda, having no internal or external protective shell or bone (unlike the nautilus, squid and cuttlefish) and eight arms each covered with suckers.
ex: Even octopuses without stylets almost certainly retain the molecular machinery necessary to build them.

s.def: The flesh of these marine molluscs eaten as food.
An organization that has many powerful branches controlled from the centre.
An instance of a player scoring a touchdown immediately followed by a successful two-point conversion, resulting in a total score of eight points.
A safety device allowing divers to share an air supply in an emergency.
To put (or attempt to put) one's fingers, hands or arms in many things or places at roughly the same time.
ex: He rises up on his wasted legs, the healer's hands octopussed on his head.
A skinny, sauced-looking gent in shorts and baseball cap wandered in through the door, his arms octopussing no less than three pre-teen girls.
I took off my shirt, standing in swim trunks, embarrassed of my tour body, my hands octopussing around the ashamed drink tickets of my gut.

s.def: To spread out in long arms or legs in many directions.
ex: The bug-eyed press octopussed to their respective word processors.
Dirt roads octopussed into the interior, where there were more dried mud and shrivelled crops.
He had attached three more on so now there were seven legs octopussing out from underneath the chair.

s.def: To plug a large number of devices into a single electric outlet.
ex: By now, the reservation had electricity so THAT had to be octopussed out to the trailers too.
It was an eight-channel audio recording snake, a bundled set of cables with eight plugs octopussing out of either end.

s.def: To grow in use vastly beyond what was originally intended.
ex: The performance of it, however, did not improve, being octopussed by centuries-old not-to-move bureaucracy.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw Proto-Hellenic *oktṓ Ancient Greek ὀκτώ (oktṓ)bor. Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw Proto-Italic *oktō Latin octōbor. English octo- English syllable English octosyllable From octo- + syllable.

s.def: line of verse with eight syllables

ety: Borrowed from French octroi, from Middle French octroy, alteration of Old French otroi, from otroier (“to grant”), from Late Latin auctōrizāre.

s.def: A privilege granted by the sovereign authority, such as the exclusive right of trade granted to a guild or society; a concession.
A tax levied in money or kind at the gate of a French city on articles brought within the walls.

ety: By surface analysis, oct- + -u- + -ple.

s.def: eightfold
An eightfold amount or number
To increase or multiply something by eight.
To increase eightfold.

ety: Borrowed from Late Latin octuplicātus, perfect passive participle of octuplicō or formed by blend of octuple + duplicate, either way, see -ate (noun-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix).

s.def: A set of eight like or identical things.
ex: A unit's actual transfer will be brought about through the issuance of a Form S-46, "Transfer Order," which is made up in octuplicate.
Letters of nomination together with supporting documents must be submitted in octuplicate to Earl G. Hammond, Department of Food Technology […]

s.def: To make eight copies of something

ety: Derived from the Latin oculāris (“of the eye”), from oculus (“eye”).

s.def: Of, or relating to the eye, or the sense of sight
ex: The medication may have adverse ocular side effects.
It took some time after he lost his eye for him to receive his ocular prosthesis.

s.def: Resembling the eye.
ex: ocular markings on the wings of a butterfly

s.def: Seen by, or seeing with, the eye; visual.
The eyepiece of a microscope or other optical instrument, i.e., the optical element closest to the eye.
Any of the scales forming the margin of a reptile's eye.

ety: From French oculiste (“oculist”), from Latin oculus (“eye”).

s.def: An eye doctor; an ophthalmologist or optometrist.

ety: From Latin oculus (“eye”) + linctus (“licked”), past participle of lingo (“to lick”).

s.def: A paraphilia involving licking the eyeballs.

ety: Borrowed from French odalisque, from Ottoman Turkish اوطهلق (odalık, “chambermaid”), from اوده (oda, “room”).

s.def: A female slave in a harem, especially one in the Ottoman seraglio.
ex: They grew fat, but successfully resisted the enticing odalisques with whom they were confronted.
The Sector is borne in a padded Waggon, like some mechanickal Odalisque.

s.def: An erotic painting of a woman, usually nude, reclining in a luxurious or exotic setting.
A desirable or sexually attractive woman.

ety: From Middle English odde, od (“odd (not even); leftover after division into pairs”), from Old Norse oddi (“odd, third or additional number; triangle”), from oddr (“point of a weapon”), from Proto-Germanic *uzdaz (“point”), from Proto-Indo-European *wes- (“to stick, prick, pierce, sting”) + *dʰeh₁- (“to set, place”). Cognate to Icelandic oddi (“triangle, point of land, odd number”), Swedish udda (“odd”), udd (“a point”), Danish od (“point of weapon”) and odde (“a headland, point”), Norwegian Bok…

s.def: Numerically indivisible by two.
ex: The product of two odd numbers is also odd.

s.def: Differing from what is usual, ordinary or expected.
ex: She slept in, which was very odd.

s.def: Without a corresponding mate in a pair or set; unmatched; (of a pair or set) mismatched.
ex: Optimistically, he had a corner of a drawer for odd socks.
My cat Fluffy has odd eyes: one blue and one brown.

s.def: Left over, remaining after the rest have been paired or grouped.
ex: I'm the odd one out.

s.def: Left over or remaining (as a small amount) after counting, payment, etc.
ex: Third was my college loan of five thousand dollars and some odd change.

s.def: Scattered; occasional, infrequent; not forming part of a set or pattern.
ex: I don't speak Latin well, so in hearing a dissertation in Latin, I would only be able to make out the odd word of it.
but for the odd exception

s.def: Not regular or planned.
ex: He's only worked odd jobs.

s.def: Used or employed for odd jobs.
ex: At about 14 he rises a step by getting the 'odd' horse and cart, and does all the small carting work about the farm.
There is also the “orra man who, like the odd horse, is kept busy on odd jobs.

s.def: Numbered with an odd number.
ex: How do I print only the odd pages?

s.def: About, approximately; somewhat more than (an approximated round number).
ex: There were thirty-odd people in the room.

s.def: Any integer that produces a noninteger when divided by two. (This entry is a translation hub.)

ety: Etymology tree English odd Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-ts Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts Latin -itāsder. Old French -itebor. Middle English -ite English -ity English oddity From odd + -ity.

s.def: An odd or strange thing or opinion.
A strange person; an oddball.
Strangeness.
plural of oddment
A variety of miscellaneous things.

ety: From odd (“uneven, strange”).

s.def: The ratio of the probability of an event happening to that of it not happening.
ex: I'd say the odds are strongly in favor of the sun rising tomorrow morning.

s.def: The ratio of winnings to stake in betting situations.
ex: I looked at the odds given by all bookmakers.

s.def: An advantage given to a weaker opponent in order to equalize the game when playing casually, usually by removing one of the stronger player's pieces or by giving the weaker player more time.
ex: She beat me with knight odds but lost with rook odds.
The grandmaster gave his opponents significant time odds, of one minute versus ten minutes.
The resulting match of fourteen games was won by Mr. Maurian, who had scored all the Knight-odds parties and the majority of the even-term ones!

s.def: plural of odd

ety: From Middle French ode, from Late Latin ōda, from Ancient Greek ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”). Doublet of Aoede.

s.def: A short poetical composition proper to be set to music or sung; a lyric poem; especially, now, a poem characterized by sustained noble sentiment and appropriate dignity of style.
ex: write an ode to someone

s.def: An odonate; a dragonfly or damselfly.

ety: Borrowed from Russian Оде́сса (Odéssa), named after an Ancient Greek settlement thought to have been located nearby. Ancient Greek Ὀδησσός (Odēssós). Compare Ukrainian Оде́са (Odésa). The city was on the former Turkish territory of Yedisan, which may have influenced the choice of name. Yedisan means "seven titles" i.e. tribes, from yedi + san.

s.def: city in Ukraine

A locale in Canada:
A locale in the United States:

ety: From Middle English odious, from Old French odieus, from Latin odiōsus, from odium (“hate”).

s.def: Arousing or meriting strong dislike, aversion, or intense displeasure.
ex: Scrubbing the toilets in the bar at the end of a Saturday night is an odious task.
You told a lie, an odious damned lie: / Upon my soul, a lie, a wicked lie!
I own no crime, unless it be a crime to've hindered you from perpetrating that which would have made you odious to mankind, at least the fairest half.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed-der. Proto-Italic *odjom Latin odiumlbor. English odium Learned borrowing from Latin odium, from Proto-Italic *odjom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed-.

s.def: Hatred; dislike.
ex: His conduct brought him into odium, or, brought odium upon him.
‘I warned you, if you give evidence against your husband, you will be shunned. You will be held in odium. You will be alone.’

s.def: The quality that provokes hatred; offensiveness.
ex: She threw the odium of the fact on me.

ety: From French odomètre, from Ancient Greek ὁδός (hodós, “road, path, way”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”), equivalent to odo- + -meter.

s.def: An instrument, usually embedded within the speedometer of a vehicle, that measures the distance the vehicle has traveled since production.
A wheel used by surveyors, which registers distance traveled.

ety: Ancient Greek ὀδών (odṓn, “tooth”) + -oid

s.def: Resembling a tooth, especially in shape
A separate bone, in many reptiles, corresponding to the odontoid process.

ety: From Middle English odour, borrowed from Anglo-Norman odour, from Old French odor, from Latin odor. Cognates * Swedish odör (“bad smell”)

s.def: Any smell, whether fragrant or offensive.
A strong, pervasive quality.
Esteem.
Something which produces a scent; incense, a perfume.

ety: From Latin. By surface analysis, odor + -i- (“bearing, carrying”) + -ferous.

s.def: Having an odor or fragrance.
ex: Frankini disguised as Mr. Beefo: "Who wants to get out and smell that wet beef?" Captain Man: "Me, I do, Me! Oh yes, so odoriferous!"

ety: Etymology tree English odor Proto-Indo-European *lewh₁- Proto-Indo-European *lewHs-der. Proto-Germanic *leusaną Proto-Germanic *lausaz Proto-Germanic *-lausaz Proto-West Germanic *-laus Old English -lēas Middle English -les English -less English odorless From odor + -less.

ety: From Middle English odorous, from Medieval Latin odōrōsus, equivalent to odor + -ous.

s.def: Having a distinctive odor.
ex: The table was piled with odorous lilies.

ety: From Ancient Greek Ὀδυσσεύς (Odusseús). Doublet of Ulysses.

s.def: The son of Laertes and Anticlea and father of Telemachus. A Greek leader during the Trojan War, he was responsible for the Trojan horse. He was also king of Ithaca, hero of the Iliad, and protagonist of the Odyssey.
A male given name from Ancient Greek.

ety: From Odyssey, from Ancient Greek Ὀδυσσεία (Odusseía, “the story of Odysseus”).

s.def: An extended adventurous voyage, usually in search of home.
ex: Many have been sharing cartoons praying for a successful conclusion to the Wild Boar team's odyssey, hoping that it will end in their safe rescue.

s.def: An intellectual or spiritual quest.

ety: From Oedipus + -al.

s.def: Of or relating to the Oedipus complex.

ety: Named after Oedipus in Greek mythology, who unwittingly killed his father and married his mother.

s.def: In Freudian theory, the complex of emotions aroused in a child by an unconscious sexual desire for the parent of the opposite sex.

ety: From oenology + -ist or oeno- + -logist.

ety: From Ancient Greek οἰσοφάγος (oisophágos), from οἴσω (oísō), future form of φέρω (phérō, “to carry”) + ἔφαγον (éphagon, “to eat”).

s.def: The tube that carries food from the pharynx to the stomach.
ex: Graham, who lived in Somersham, Cambridgeshire, donated his oesophagus to the MRC cancer unit at Cambridge University, for research.

Nothing may come of these ideas, yet their potential should not be dismissed.

s.def: Expressing composition, substance.

s.def: Introducing subject matter.

ex: Not tarrying long enough in the brain to be subject to reflection, the next sensations, of course, obliterate them.

s.def: That keeps promises and tells the truth.
ex: She never needed to show them to us — we knew, just as the adults did, that Dadi was a woman of her word.

ety: Unknown; perhaps from an African language (possibly Yoruba ófé (“to evade, disappear”)). Pig Latin for foe, though popularly posited, is probably not accurate. s.def: A white person.

ex: He drove off in a cloud of smoke.

ex: Please switch off the light when you leave.

ex: He bit off the end of the carrot.

ex: 3 off 20 amp fuses

Inoperative, disabled.

ex: The party's off because the hostess is sick.

s.def: Not fitted; not being worn.
ex: Your feet will feel better once those tight boots are off.

ex: I felt that his comments were a bit off.

s.def: Not vigilant; unprepared; inattentive.
ex: His sudden appearance at the office caught her completely off guard.

ex: We can build a specialized part for you, but an off-the-shelf product will probably cost less.

ety: From Middle English offal, offall, offalle (“offal, refuse, scrap waste”), equivalent to off- + fall. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Oufal (“offal”), West Frisian ôffal (“offal”), Dutch afval (“waste, refuse”), German Low German Offall (“offal”), German Abfall (“waste, refuse”), Danish affald (“waste, refuse”), Swedish avfall (“waste, refuse”), Old English offeallan (“to cut off”).

ex: All the insides clean and compact, coming out all together. Nick tossed the offal ashore for the minks to find.

A dead body; carrion.
That which is thrown away as worthless or unfit for use; refuse; rubbish.

ety: From off- + beat; not following the beat (e.g., of a drum that sounds out cadence).

s.def: The beats not normally accented in a measure.
ex: The congregation clapped along on the offbeat.

s.def: An unconventional person, someone who does not follow the beat, who chooses not to conform.
ex: No one dignified such offbeats by responding to their outcries. Today, the "knockers of progress" have become a force that cannot be ignored.

s.def: Unusual; unconventional; not ordinary.
ex: He has such an offbeat sense of humor that hardly anyone finds his jokes amusing.

ety: From Middle English ofcasten, equivalent to off- + cast. Cognate with Danish afkaste (“to shed”), Swedish avkasta (“to crop, throw off, yield”). The noun is possibly derived from Middle English ofcast (“the refuse of plants”).

To remove from the cast of a production.
ex: The experiment to offcast Davis began in 1937 with That Certain Woman; "She's a lady," we are told.
[...] and Paramount was not inclined to offcast its stars, the story was dropped.

s.def: That which is rejected as useless.

ety: From Middle French offendre, from Latin offendō (“strike, blunder, commit an offense”), from ob- (“against”) + *fendō (“strike”).

s.def: To hurt the feelings of; to displease; to make angry; to insult.
ex: Your accusations offend me deeply.

s.def: To feel or become offended; to take insult.
ex: Don't worry. I don't offend easily.

s.def: To physically harm, pain.
ex: Strong light offends the eye.

s.def: To annoy, cause discomfort or resent.
ex: Physically enjoyable frivolity can still offend the conscience

s.def: To sin, transgress divine law or moral rules.
To transgress or violate a law or moral requirement.
ex: Wearing faded baggy offends against the club's rules of proper dress.

s.def: To cause to stumble; to cause to sin or to fall.
ex: "If any man offend not (stumbles not, is not tripped up) in word, the same is a perfect man."

ety: From Middle French offensif, from offendre + -if by analogy with défensif. Offendre is from Latin offendere (“to offend”); see offend.

s.def: Causing offense; arousing a visceral reaction of disgust, anger, hatred, sadness, or indignation.
ex: Some people find pornography offensive.
An offensive smell.

s.def: Having to do with play directed at scoring.
ex: The offensive coordinator is responsible for ordering all rushing plays.

s.def: Relating to an offense or attack, as opposed to defensive.
ex: The army's offensive capabilities. An offensive weapon.

s.def: An attack.
ex: The Marines today launched a major offensive.

s.def: The posture of attacking or being able to attack.
ex: He took the offensive in the press, accusing his opponent of corruption.

ety: From Middle English offer, from Old English offrian (“offer or make a sacrifice”) rather than from Old French offre (“offer”), from offrir (“to offer”), from Latin offerō (“to present, bring before”). s.def: A proposal that has been made.
ex: What's in his offer?

ex: According to Russian deputy prime minister Dmitrii Kozak, every ruble spent on preparations for the Sochi Olympics has been justified.

ety: From Latin Olympus, from Ancient Greek Ὄλυμπος (Ólumpos), likely of Pre-Greek origin.

s.def: The highest mountain in Greece; in Ancient Greek mythology the home of the gods.

s.def: A country in West Asia in the Middle East. Official name: Sultanate of Oman. Capital: Muscat.

s.def: A male given name from Arabic.
Omar bin al-Khattab, second Sunni Islamic caliph and a companion of Muhammad

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin omāsum.

s.def: The third compartment of the stomach of a ruminant; the lining of said compartment, regarded as a foodstuff.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dʰeǵʰ- Proto-Indo-European *-ōm Proto-Indo-European *dʰéǵʰōm Proto-Indo-European *-ō Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰmṓ Proto-Italic *hemō Latin hemō Latin homō Latin hominem Old Spanish omne Spanish hombrebor. s.def: A Spanish card game, usually played by three people. It involves forty cards, omitting the ranks of 8, 9 and 10.
ex: When ombre calls, his hand and heart are free, / And, joined to two, he fails not to make three.

s.def: A large Mediterranean food fish, Umbrina cirrosa.
Alternative spelling of ombré (“a gradual blending of one color hue to another”).

ety: Borrowed from Swedish ombudsman (equivalent to ombud (“representative, proxy”) + man), from Old Norse umboðsmaðr.

s.def: An appointed official whose duty is to investigate complaints, generally on behalf of individuals such as consumers or taxpayers, against institutions such as companies and government departments.

A designated internal mediator in an organization whose duty is to assist members with conflict resolution and other problems and to serve as an independent consultant to recommend changes to policies or procedures to improve organization effectiveness, efficiency, and humaneness.

ety: From Middle English, from Ancient Greek ὦ μέγα (ô méga), meaning “great ω” (omega is a long vowel in Ancient Greek).

s.def: The twenty-fourth letter of the Classical and the Modern Greek alphabet, and the twenty-eighth letter of the Old and the Ancient Greek alphabet, i.e. the last letter of every Greek alphabet. Uppercase version: Ω; lowercase: ω.
ex: The fact that the letter was incised above the line indicates that it is probably an omega.

s.def: The end; the final, last or ultimate in a sequence.
ex: alpha and omega
I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End.

s.def: Angular velocity; symbol: ω.
ex: The ratio between the rho and omega cross section is obtained.

s.def: A transfinite ordinal number referring to the next position after ordering a countably infinite set.
An omega male.
The percentage change in an option value divided by the percentage change in the underlying asset's price.
In omegaverse fiction, a person of a submissive secondary sex driven by biology, magic, or other means to bond with an alpha, with males of this type often being able to get pregnant.
ex: Often omegas go into heat and release pheromones that drive alphas wild.

s.def: Ultimate; of the highest degree. Massive, ineffable.
ex: Omega props, dude.

s.def: Ultimately, most, supremely.
ex: Whatever your plan is, I just think this idea's omega stupid. Ain't you got something better?

s.def: US standard spelling of omelette.

ety: First attested in 1611; borrowed from French omelette, see which for further etymology.

s.def: A dish made with beaten eggs cooked in a frying pan without stirring, flipped over to cook on both sides, and sometimes filled or topped with other foodstuffs, for example cheese or chives.
ex: She had never meant to confide in him — certainly not here, eating omelette and cheese sauce — but that look seemed to demand a confidence.
She stayed to lunch that day, eating omelette and peas in the kitchen, followed by treacle tart.

s.def: A form of shellcode that searches the address space for multiple small blocks of data ("eggs") and recombines them into a larger block to be executed.

ety: From Latin ōmen (“foreboding, omen”).

s.def: Something which portends or is perceived to portend either a good or evil event or circumstance in the future, or which causes a foreboding; a portent or augury.
ex: The ghost's appearance was an ill omen.
A rise in imports might be an omen of economic recovery.
The egg has, during the span of history, represented mystery, magic, medicine, food and omen.

s.def: A thing of prophetic significance.
ex: A sign of ill omen.

s.def: To be an omen of.
To divine or predict from omens.

ety: Borrowed from Latin ōmentum.

s.def: Either of two folds of the peritoneum that support the viscera.

ety: From Latin omicron, from Koine Greek ὂ μῑκρόν (ò mīkrón, “little o”), named in contrast with omega (“big o”). The uncommon form omicra is similarly borrowed from Latin and Greek. The use for designating stars in a constellation—typically in order of apparent brightness—began with Johann Bayer's 1603 Uranometria.

s.def: The 15th letter of the Classical and Modern Greek alphabets (16th in Ancient and Old Greek), used in ordering lists as in naming (astronomy) the 15th star of a constellation or (epidemiology) the 15th discovered major variant of a disease.
ex: The E serves both for the Epsilon and Eta; the O, both for the Omicron and Omega, and likewise for the diphthong OΥ.
... They include Mira itself (omicron Ceti) which can be seen shortly before dawn.

s.def: Ellipsis of Omicron variant.

ety: From Latin ōminōsus (“full of foreboding”), from ōmen (“forbidden fruit, omen”), from Old Latin osmen, of uncertain origin, with many origins proposed (see ōmen).

s.def: Specifically, giving indication of a coming ill; being an evil omen
ex: California poll support for Jerry Brown's tax increases has ominous implications for U.S. taxpayers too Los Angeles Times Headline April 25, 2011

s.def: Of or pertaining to an omen or to omens; being or exhibiting an omen; significant.

ety: From Middle English omissioun, from Old French omission, from Late Latin omissio, omissionem, from Latin omitto.

s.def: The act of omitting.
ex: Scots was not ‘banned’ outright — impossible anyway with so many Scots-speaking teachers but, like Gaelic, marginalised by omission.

s.def: The act of neglecting to perform an action one has an obligation to do.
ex: E&O insurance (for errors and omissions) covers both errors of commission and errors of omission.

s.def: An instance of those acts, or the thing left out thereby; something deleted or left out.
ex: The suspicious omissions in the new edition of the book attracted claims of censorship.

s.def: Something not done or neglected.
ex: The lack of a sponge count was an omission by the surgical team.

s.def: The shortening of a word or phrase, using an apostrophe ( ' ) to replace the missing letters, often used to approximate the sound of speech or a specific dialect.

ety: At least by 1422, from late Middle English omitten, borrowed from Latin omittō (“to let go”), from ob- + mittō (“to send”), but also had the connotations “to fail to perform” and “to neglect”.

s.def: To leave out or exclude.
To fail to perform.
To delete or remove; to strike.
To neglect or take no notice of.

ety: Clipping of omnivore.

s.def: A person or animal who is not vegan; one with no particular dietary restrictions.
ex: A plant-muncher starts dating an omni, engages them in thought-provoking conversations about veganism, […]
An 'omni' pub that's 'herbi'-friendly, […]

s.def: An omnidirectional microphone.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₃ep-der. Proto-Italic *opnis Latin omnis Latin omnibuslbor. French omnibusbor. English omnibus Borrowed from French (voiture) omnibus (“(carriage) for all”), from Latin omnibus (“for all”), dative plural of omnis (“all”).

s.def: A bus (vehicle for transporting large numbers of people along roads).
ex: "Please," his voice quavered through the foul brown air, "Please, is that an omnibus?" / "Omnibus est," said the driver, without turning round.
Baldrick, I want you to take this [money] and go out, and buy a turkey so large you'd think its mother had been rogered by an omnibus.

s.def: An anthology of previously released material linked together by theme or author, especially in book form.
ex: This work is an omnibus containing all books in the Remembrance of Earth’s Past series.

s.def: A broadcast programme consisting of all of the episodes of a serial that have been shown in the previous week.
ex: The omnibus edition of The Archers is broadcast every Sunday morning at 11:00.

s.def: A stamp issue, usually commemorative, that appears simultaneously in several countries as a joint issue.
An assistant waiter.
an omnibus box.
Containing multiple items.
ex: The legislature enacted an omnibus appropriations bill.
The inventors face a similar uphill battle in their fight against the omnibus bill.

s.def: Of a transportation service, calling at every station, as opposed to express; local.
To combine (legislative bills, etc.) into a single package.
ex: In the tax levy measure were omnibused all appropriations for the maintenance of government for the fiscal year.

s.def: To drive an omnibus.

ety: Inherited from Middle English omnipotent(e), from Old French omnipotent, from Latin omnipotēns, omnipotentem.

s.def: Having unlimited power, force or authority.
ex: , omnivalent
Near-synonyms: plenipotent, plenipotentiary, omnicompetent
All the spirits of the elements bowed down before him; but the future was still hidden from his eyes, and Death was omnipotent.

s.def: Describing a cell (especially a stem cell) that is capable of developing into any type of cell or forming any type of tissue (also called a totipotent cell).
Arrant.
An omnipotent being.

ety: From Medieval Latin omnisciens (“all-knowing”), from Latin omnis (“all”) + sciens (“knowing”) (further analysable via scient).

s.def: Having total knowledge.
ex: The story was narrated from an omniscient point of view.
The Abrahamic God is omniscient.
For me, anything is possible. I am omniscient and omnipotent, extremely vain, and, what is more, I come in a handy self-carrying package.

s.def: One who has total knowledge.
ex: Those blind omniscients , those almighty slaves , Untenanting creation of its God

ety: From the Latin omnivorus. By surface analysis, omni- + -vore.

s.def: An animal which is able to consume both plants (like a herbivore) and meat (like a carnivore).
ex: Bears are omnivores: they can eat plants, but they also eat fish.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₃ep-der. Proto-Italic *opnis Latin omnisder. English omni- English -vorous English omnivorous From omni- + -vorous.

s.def: Having a diet which is neither exclusively carnivorous nor exclusively herbivorous.
Having an interest in a variety of subjects.
ex: He was omnivorous in his appetite for knowledge, quite catholic in his range of interests […]

s.def: All-consuming.
Of a parasite: attacking many species; not confined to a single host plant.

ety: From omphalo- + -cele.

s.def: A hernia of the navel.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂en-der. Proto-Germanic *an Proto-West Germanic *ana Old English on Middle English on English on From Middle English on, from Old English on, an (“on, upon, onto, in, into”), from Proto-West Germanic *ana, from Proto-Germanic *ana (“on, at”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂en- (“on, onto”). s.def: Indicating position or location.
ex: A vase of flowers stood on the table.

The parrot was sitting on Jim's shoulder.

s.def: Expressing figurative placement, burden, or attachment.

I put a bet on the winning horse.

s.def: Denoting physical contact or interaction with an object, such as impact or application of force.
ex: tug on the rope; push hard on the door

s.def: Supported by (the specified part of itself).
ex: A table can't stand on two legs.
After resting on his elbows, he stood on his toes, then walked on his heels.

s.def: At (a certain position within a sequence).
ex: I'm on question four.

s.def: At or during the date or day of.
ex: Born on the 4th of July.
On Sunday I'm busy. I'll see you on Monday.
Can I see you on a different day?

s.def: At (a given time after the start of something).
ex: Smith scored again on twelve minutes, doubling Mudchester Rovers' lead.
The Spain striker had given Chelsea the lead on 29 minutes but was shown a straight red card 10 minutes later for a rash challenge on Mark Gower.

s.def: At (an instant or cusp).
ex: on the stroke of midnight; on the "B" of "Bang!"
on the point of leaving; on the verge of giving up

s.def: Dealing with the subject of; about; concerning.
ex: I was reading a book on history.

I have no opinion on this subject.

s.def: Indicating a means or medium.
ex: I saw it on television.
Can't you see I'm on the phone?
My favorite shows are on BBC America.

s.def: Without having eaten.
Speaking or acting for.
ex: On behalf of all those present, may I thank you for a well-executed presentation.

ety: From Middle English on fote, from Old English on fōte (“on foot”), equivalent to on + foot.

s.def: On the move; astir.
On one's feet; walking, jogging or running but not in a vehicle or on the back of an animal.
ex: The pub's not far: let's go on foot.

s.def: In progress or in preparation; active, in operation.
ex: [W]ithin a short time it was generally believed at Naples, that a treaty of marriage was on foot between Zeluco and the young lady in question […].
‘I didn't know anything of this sort was on foot.’ Brangwen smiled awkwardly.

s.def: Being friendly; having good relations.
Without prior consideration; spontaneously, impulsively.
ex: Near-synonym: on a whim

s.def: Based on debatable inference; in theory; by appearances only.
ex: On paper they're perfect for each other, but it's been six months and their relationship is already on the rocks.
Hutchinson, the current champion at 50 miles, is on paper the fastest rider in the field for Sunday's event

s.def: In writing, particularly handwritten or printed as opposed to digital.
ex: During the final exam, students are allowed to bring their computer science notes that are on paper.

s.def: Officially; de jure.
Of a convicted criminal: on parole.
ex: This means you can vote even if you are in jail or prison, or “on paper” (on probation, parole or extended supervision) for a misdemeanor.

s.def: Feeling sharp anticipation or anxiety; in a state of suspense.
ex: Merlin hesitated a moment or two, and I was on pins and needles during that little while.
I was on pins and needles of expectation and curiosity.

s.def: By design, as opposed to by accident; intentionally; deliberately.
ex: That wasn't an accident! You did it on purpose!

s.def: In order to (do something); with the objective that.
ex: I send this to the town, on purpose to have it reach you by the earliest post […].

s.def: Immediately when sighted.
ex: I recognized him on sight.

s.def: Immediately upon coming to one's attention.
ex: He dismissed the idea on sight.

s.def: cause for a fight, immediately upon encounter without deliberation.
ex: If he keeps talking crap about me, its on sight.

s.def: Withholding labor as a protest, in order to effect change in management or government.
Due to face the next delivery from the bowler.
While in the air, without having touched the ground.
ex: Jones caught the ball on the fly.

s.def: Spontaneously or extemporaneously; done as one goes, or during another activity.
ex: The software program has a table of values for some results, but calculates others on the fly.
The only process that yields problem-solving on the fly is experiential.

s.def: On the move.
ex: The Owl is flying high, frightening to the eye. The Rattler is nearby, Cool is on the fly. Danger is his business.

s.def: Constantly alert, intent on finding something or someone.
ex: I'm on the lookout for a good example of a Roman dinar from the 1st century. Let me know if you hear of one anywhere.

s.def: Not incarcerated or in captivity; not under control.
Out on a spree, or in search of adventure.
ex: Sometimes he dispensed water to men who “looked as if they had been on the loose all night.”

s.def: Earning a living by prostitution.
From another point of view.
ex: Well yes, it was quite a good bargain; on the other hand, do we really need one?

w: on the tip of one's tongue

s.def: Known but not quite able to be recalled.
ex: Her name is on the tip of my tongue: it's Kathy, or Karen, or something.

s.def: Punctually or according to the schedule.
ex: The train arrived on time for the first time this week.

s.def: By installments, payments over a period of time.
ex: They bought their dining-room furniture on time.

s.def: By a player's running out of time.
ex: Smith beat Jones on time.

ety: From Middle English onager, onagir (“wild ass; military catapult”), from Anglo-Norman onager, Middle French onager, onagre, Old French onager, onagre (“wild ass; military catapult”) (modern French onagre), from Late Latin onager (“large siege engine”), Latin onager (“wild ass”), from Hellenistic Ancient Greek ὄναγρος (ónagros, “wild ass”), Byzantine Ancient Greek ὄναγρος (ónagros, “large siege engine”), from ὄνος (ónos, “ass”) + ἄγριος (ágrios, “wild”) (from ᾰ̓γρός (ăgrós, “countryside; field”)…

s.def: The Asiatic wild ass or hemione (Equus hemionus), an animal of the horse family native to Asia; specifically, the Persian onager, Persian wild ass, or Persian zebra (Equus hemionus onager).
ex: One of the onagers, however, having hurt its leg, could not be harnessed at present, and a few days' rest was necessary.

s.def: A military engine acting like a sling which threw stones from a bag or wooden bucket powered by the torsion from a bundle of ropes or sinews operated by machinery; a torsion catapult.

ety: From Onan + -ism. In the Book of Genesis, Onan, son of Judah, in fulfillment of the laws of levirate marriage was to impregnate his brother Er's widow, Tamar, in order to raise offspring from the union in his brother's name. In order to avoid raising descendants for his late brother, however, Onan "spilled his semen on the ground when he went in to his brother's wife, so that he would not give offspring to his brother" (Genesis 38:9).

s.def: Masturbation.
Ejaculating outside the vagina during intercourse; (the performing of) coitus interruptus.

ety: From Middle English ones, from Old English ānes, a remodelling (after ān (“one”)) of ǣnes, itself an extension of ǣne (“once”) with the genitive suffix -es. Equivalent to one + -s. Cognate with Saterland Frisian enst, insen (“once”), West Frisian iens (“once”), Dutch eens (“once”), German Low German eens, ins (“once”), German einst (“once”). More at one (including regarding the development of the pronunciation) and -s.

s.def: One and only one time.
ex: I have only once eaten pizza.

s.def: Formerly; during some period in the past.
ex: He was once the most handsome man around.
I once had a motorbicycle.
Once I didn't drive a big car, but now I own an all-terrain 4WD.

s.def: At any time; ever.
ex: If the facts once became known, we'd be in trouble.
Once bring in the police and what is inevitably bound to follow? There will be calls and interrogations and cross-questionings […]

s.def: One day, someday.
ex: The wisdom of God thought fit to acquaint David with that court which we shall once govern.

s.def: Multiplied by one: indicating that a number is multiplied by one.
ex: Once three is three.

s.def: As soon as; when; after.
ex: Near-synonym: immediately
We'll get a move on once we find the damn car keys!
Once you have obtained the elven bow, return to the troll bridge and trade it for the sleeping potion.

s.def: Obsolete form of ounce.

don't spend it all at once
once a man, twice a boy
once a man, twice a child
once a woman, twice a child

s.def: Again, once more, one more time.

s.def: Conclusively, finally, permanently.
ex: They replaced the entire door, in hopes of correcting the sticking and squeaking once and for all.

s.def: One is cautious if one has been hurt in the past.

ety: See blue moon. First use appears c. 1833. See citation below.

s.def: Very rarely; very infrequently.
A long time ago; at some time in the past (a traditional beginning of children's stories, especially fairy tales).
ex: Once upon a time, in a faraway land, there lived a beautiful princess.
There was once upon a time a charcoal-burner who had a son, and he was also a charcoal-burner.
Once upon a time, there was a Goblin Queen And she lived in a grand palace...

s.def: Formerly.

ety: Borrowed from Spanish oncilla, diminutive of onza (“snow leopard”).

s.def: A small spotted felid, of species Leopardus tigrinus, found in the tropical rainforests of Central America and South America.
