s.def: The branch of medicine concerned with tumors, including study of their development, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention.

ety: From Middle English on comynge, oncomynge, oncoomynge; equivalent to on- + coming (noun).

s.def: Approach, onset
ex: Some man that wayfaring was stood by housedoor at night's oncoming.
Instead, the sound of muffled drums Inside myself: I have to lean And listen as my strength succumbs, To hear what these oncomings mean.

s.def: approaching; coming closer
ex: Look carefully before pulling out into oncoming traffic.
A bitter easterly breeze blew with a threat of oncoming winter.
Because it had not taken place immediately, the oncoming fight would lack spontaneity; it would be calculated, uninspired, and deadly.

s.def: present participle and gerund of oncome

ety: From New Latin onco- (“tumor”), from Ancient Greek ὄγκος (ónkos, “lump, mass, bulk”) + -tic.

s.def: Relating to osmotic pressure caused by the presence of colloids.

ety: PIE word *h₁óynos Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ís? s.def: The number represented by the Arabic numeral 1; the numerical value equal to that cardinal number.
ex: In some religions, there is more than one god.
In many cultures, a baby turns one year old a year after its birth.
One person, one vote.

s.def: The digit or figure 1.
The first positive number in the set of natural numbers.
The cardinality of the smallest nonempty set.
The ordinality of an element which has no predecessor, usually called first or number one.
One thing (among a group of others); one member of a group.
ex: Any one of the boys.
Every one of the bank’s employees.
A good driver is one who drives carefully.

s.def: The first mentioned of two things or people, as opposed to the other.
ex: She offered him an apple and an orange; he took (the) one and left the other.
I am one of the few women who've climbed Everest.

s.def: Any person (applying to people in general).
ex: One’s guilt may trouble one, but it is best not to let oneself be troubled by things which cannot be changed. One shouldn’t be too quick to judge.
My neighbor talks to one like a teacher.

s.def: Any person, entity or thing.
ex: "driver", noun: one who drives.

s.def: Used to briefly refer to a noun phrase understood by context
ex: I need some ones to make change.

s.def: Used of a reciprocal relationship among a group of two or more people or things; compare each other.
ex: The raw recruits helped one another get over the first few days.

s.def: Individually in succession.
ex: The passengers escaped through the hatch one by one.

s.def: At some unspecified time in the past.

ex: Changing the oil lubricates the engine and removes debris in one fell swoop.

Possession of absolute knowledge would ossify the human spirit, quenching human creativity;

s.def: To grow (or cause to grow) formulaic and permanent.
ex: This accidental repartition gets repeated, develops advantages of its own, and gradually ossifies into a systematic division of labour.
Now, in turn, we apply a revolutionary critique that […] ossifies into a rhetoric to become "the monstrous Latin of a monstrous church."
[T]he charge threatens to ossify into conventional wisdom before the movie's audience can get to theaters to see how misguided it is.

s.def: To calcify.
ex: The cartilages become brittle, and in many instances are ossified; the ligaments are rendered harder, but are less capable of resisting extension.

ety: From Late Latin ossuārium (“charnel house”), from ossuārius (“of or for bones”), from compound of Latin os (“bone”) + adjectival suffix -ārius (“of, related to”).

ety: Borrowed from French ostensible, formed with the suffix -ible, from Latin ostensus, the past participle of ostendō (“show”), itself from obs- (“in front of”) (akin to ob- (“in the way”)) + tendō (“stretch”) (akin to Ancient Greek τείνω (teínō)). Cf. ostentatious.

s.def: Apparent, evident; meant for open display.

ex: The ostensible reason for his visit to New York was to see his mother, but the real reason was to get to the Yankees game the next day.

ex: I overestimated the number of attendees, and bought far too much food for the party.

s.def: An estimate that is too high.
ex: The employment projection for the metropolitan area for 1985 was an overestimate by about 12 percent.

ety: From over- + expose.

s.def: To expose excessively.
To provide excessive publicity or reporting regarding (a person, event, etc.).
To expose (film) to light during the development process for a longer time than is required to accurately produce the image.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *úp Proto-Indo-European *-er Proto-Indo-European *upér Proto-Germanic *uber Old English ofer- Middle English over- English over- English exposure English overexposure From over- + exposure.

s.def: Excessive exposure.
Of a famous person, excessive publicity, publication or reporting regarding that person.
Exposure of film to light during the development process for a longer time than is required to accurately produce the image.
Fishing that reduces the stock of remaining fish in an area to below that which is acceptable.
ex: Most of the overfishings in the international sense are a product of misuse.

ety: From Middle English overflowen, from Old English oferflōwan, equivalent to over- + flow.

s.def: (transitive) to fill beyond the limits of
The spillage resultant from overflowing.
An outlet for escape of excess material.
Excess, superabundance
The situation where a value exceeds the available numeric range.
To cover with a liquid, literally or figuratively.
ex: The flash flood overflowed most of the parkland and some homes.

s.def: To flow over the brim of (a container).
ex: The river overflowed the levee into the road.
The shadows had begun to overflow Their stagnant puddles on the nightward side, When presently the roar of battle died

s.def: To be subject to a load that exceeds limits or capacity.
ex: I see and feel that I want the first requisite — a heart overflowing with Divine love towards sinners

s.def: To cause an overflow.
To (cause to) exceed the available numeric range.
ex: Calculating 255+1 will overflow an eight-bit byte.

ety: From overflow + -ing.

s.def: overflow
ex: the great overflowings and recedings of the waters

s.def: present participle and gerund of overflow

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *úp Proto-Indo-European *-er Proto-Indo-European *upér Proto-Germanic *uber Old English ofer- Middle English over- English over- English grow English overgrow From over- + grow.

s.def: To grow beyond one's boundaries or containment, or beyond the proper size.
To grow over; (of one thing) to cause (a second thing) to become overgrown (with or by the first thing).
ex: If there is ivy overgrowing things, then we shall clean it up.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *úp Proto-Indo-European *-er Proto-Indo-European *upér Proto-Germanic *uber Old English ofer- Middle English over- English over- Proto-Germanic *handuz Proto-West Germanic *handu Old English hand Middle English hond English hand English overhand From over- + hand.

s.def: Executed with the hand brought forward and down from above the shoulders.
ex: an overhand shuffle of a deck of cards

s.def: Sewn with close, vertical stitches that draw the edges of a seam together.
With the working part on top of the standing part.
Laid such that the surface of the wall to be jointed is on the opposite side of the wall from the mason, requiring the mason to lean over the wall to complete the work.
Done from below upward.
The upper hand; advantage; superiority; mastery.
ex: He had gotten thereby a great overhand on me.

s.def: In an overhand manner
Sew using an overhand stitch.
ex: Now, those little ends of the bag above the running stitches, are to be overhanded together.

ety: From Old English oferhangan, corresponding to over- + hang.

s.def: To hang over (something).
ex: Her brow was overhung with coins of gold, / That sparkled o'er the auburn of her hair [...].
At that time, the upper part of the tower overhanged its base by about fourteen feet.

s.def: To impend.
That portion of the roof structure that extends beyond the exterior walls of a building.
The volume that tips the balance between the demand and the supply toward demand lagging supply.
A fatty roll of pubis flab that hangs over one's genitals; a FUPA.
Anything that overhangs or protrudes over its base, such as a wave immediately before breaking, or a protruding cliff or rock wall.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *úp Proto-Indo-European *-er Proto-Indo-European *upér Proto-Germanic *uber Old English ofer- Middle English over- English over- English haul English overhaul From over- + haul.

s.def: A major repair, renovation, or revision.
ex: The engine required a complete overhaul to run properly.

s.def: The process after the fire appears extinguished in which the firefighters search the structure for signs of hot spots that may cause the structure to reignite.
To modernize, repair, renovate, or revise completely.
ex: While the engines are dealt with in the diesel shop, their parent locomotives are overhauled in the erecting shop.

s.def: To pass, overtake, or travel past.
To keep (running rigging) clear, and see that no hitch occurs.
To search (a ship) for contraband goods.
To carry out an overhaul.

ety: From Middle English owerheved, over-hed, over hede (adverb), from Old English oferhēafod (adverb), equivalent to over- + head. Compare German Low German overhoopt, överhoopt, German überhaupt. Piecewise doublet of overchief.

s.def: Located above, especially over the head.
ex: Place your luggage in the overhead lockers.
The railway consists of some 18 miles of double track electrified on the overhead principle.

s.def: Kicked over one's own head.
The expense of a business not directly assigned to goods or services provided.
Wasted money.
Above one's head; in the sky.
ex: birds flying overhead

s.def: The items or classes of expense not directly assigned to goods or services provided.
Any cost or expenditure (monetary, time, effort or otherwise) incurred in a project or activity, which does not directly contribute to its progress or outcome.
A smash.
The ceiling of any enclosed space below decks in a vessel.
A compartment above the seats for stowing luggage in a passenger aircraft.
ex: There was no room left in the overheads for our luggage, our seats did not recline, and the washrooms were right behind us.

ety: From Middle English overheren, from Old English oferhīeran (“to overhear, hear, disobey, disregard, neglect”), equivalent to over- + hear. Cognate with Dutch overhoren (“to hear, hear about”), German überhören (“to not hear, ignore”), Danish overhøre (“to overhear”), Icelandic yfirheyra (“to hear”), Gothic *𐌿𐍆𐌰𐍂𐌷𐌰𐌿𐍃𐌾𐌰𐌽 (*ufarhausjan, “to disregard, disobey”) (in 𐌿𐍆𐌰𐍂𐌷𐌰𐌿𐍃𐌴𐌹𐌽𐍃 (ufarhauseins)).

s.def: To hear something that was not meant for one's ears.
ex: I was hanging clothes in the garden and I overheard the neighbours talking about Sheila's pregnancy.
"It is incomprehensible," replied Sir Fergus, dropping his voice so that the old man could not overhear.

s.def: simple past and past participle of overinflate
Inflated; exaggerated
ex: As a callow sixth-former with an overinflated sense of my own poetic importance, I was in need of friendly advice and encouragement.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *úp Proto-Indo-European *-er Proto-Indo-European *upér Proto-Germanic *uber Old English ofer- Middle English over- English over- English joy English overjoy From over- + joy.

s.def: To give great joy, delight or pleasure to.
ex: The prospect of writing three exams in a row without a break does not overjoy me.
This salutation ouerioyes my heart.
In overjoying me, you are grown sad;

s.def: To give too much joy to.
To take too much pleasure (in something).
ex: 1598, John Wilbye, The First Set of English Madrigals, London: Thomas Este, Madrigal , Your deeds my hart surchargd with ouerioying:
it is hard not to ouer-ioy in a sudden prosperitie, and, to vse happinesse is no lesse difficult, then to forbeare it

s.def: Very great joy.
ex: The katydids express their overjoy / Down in knee-high maturing August grasses;

s.def: Excessive joy.
ex: The knowledge that some are deprived tempers overjoy or overdesire.
The emotional extremes of overexcitement, overjoy, depression, and anxiety are all blockages in the Message Center.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *úp Proto-Indo-European *-er Proto-Indo-European *upér Proto-Germanic *uber Old English ofer- Middle English over- English over- Dutch kilbor. English kill English overkill From over- + kill.

s.def: A destructive capacity that exceeds that needed to destroy an enemy; especially with nuclear weapons.
Destruction beyond what is necessary to kill, especially in murder.
ex: For some killers with a great deal of love/hate for their victims, it [an edged weapon] is the perfect instrument for a maniacal overkill.

s.def: An unnecessary excess of whatever is needed to achieve a goal.
ex: 24 hours of TV coverage of the US election verged on overkill.
Should I give you yet more homework, or would that be overkill?

s.def: An unnecessary excess of disposal because of too high criteria of inspection.
To destroy something with more (nuclear) force than is required.
To dispose of too many items because of too-high criteria of inspection.
To do something excessive to achieve a goal.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *úp Proto-Indo-European *-er Proto-Indo-European *upér Proto-Germanic *uber Old English ofer- Middle English over- English over- English laden English overladen From over- + laden.

s.def: Packed heavily, especially beyond normal capacity; overloaded.
ex: The tray was overladen with food.
The trunk was overladen with clothes.

s.def: Burdened excessively.
ex: The student is overladen with homework.
The first-time parents are overladen with new responsibility.

s.def: past participle of overlade

ety: From over + land.

s.def: By or across land.
ex: Let's take the overland route.
So, sir. I desire of you A conduct overland to Milford Haven.

s.def: Over, across, or by land.
ex: To prevent this, he practised that none of the Companies servauntes shuld be suffered to goe overland with letters.
The packet that was coming to us overland, and that left England in July, was cut off by the wild Arabs between Aleppo and Bussora.

s.def: A trip by land between the UK and the Indian subcontinent or Australia, or between the UK and South Africa.
To transport (especially sheep or other farm animals) over land.
ex: Not long after, in 1878, Nathaniel Buchanan overlanded cattle from Queensland to Glencoe and Daly River stations in the Northern Territory.

s.def: To travel across land.
To go on a recreational expedition to a remote destination, often with the aid of an off-road vehicle.
ex: I don't think any of them had done the backpacker thing and certainly hadn't overlanded through Africa before, as we had.

ety: From over- + lap. Cognate with Dutch overlap.

s.def: To extend over and partly cover something.
ex: The mouse-mat overlapped the edge of the desk.

s.def: To co-occur, to happen at the same time.
To have an area, range, character or function in common.
ex: The two maps overlapped at the east and west edges.

s.def: Of sets: to have some elements in common.
ex: The set (all men) overlaps the set (vegetarians).

s.def: To have some similar nucleotide sequences.
An illusion of depth is created when one object partially covers another.

a situation in the game where an attacking line has more players in it than the defensive line coming to meet it. The attacking side may exploit the overlap by using their superior numbers to break the opposition's defensive line. If attackers outnumber defenders by more than one player this is oft…
The payment of a spouse's or other dependant's annuity benefits concurrently with the member's benefits, on death of the member during the guarantee period.
Something that overlaps or is overlapped.

ety: From Middle English overleyen, from Old English oferleċġan, from Proto-West Germanic *obarlaggjan, from Proto-Germanic *uberlagjaną, equivalent to over- + lay. Cognate with Saterland Frisian uurläze, úurlääse, Dutch overleggen, German Low German overleggen, överleggen, German überlegen, Swedish överlägga, Norwegian overlegge. Compare overlie.

s.def: To lay, spread, or apply (something) over or across (something else); to overspread.
ex: Near-synonyms: cover, superimpose, superpose
She will now overlay the crust with fruit.
She will now overlay fruit on top of the crust.

s.def: To overwhelm; to press excessively upon.
ex: when any country is overlaid by the multitude which live upon it

s.def: To lie over (someone, especially a child) in order to smother it; to suffocate.
ex: And this womans childe died in the night: because she ouerlaid it.
a heap of ashes that o'erlays your fire

s.def: To put an overlay on.
To bet too much money on.
ex: […] he has 'overlaid' his book, and has not succeeded in 'getting round' by bets against the other horses.

s.def: An image to be overlaid on another; a superimposition or diapositive.
A piece of paper pasted upon the tympan sheet to improve the impression by making it stronger at a particular place.
A covering over something else.
ex: The first, on January 1, 1883, was attributed to the overlay becoming surcharged with water, due to insufficient drainage, and causing a slip.

s.def: Odds which are set higher than expected or warranted. Favorable odds.
A horse going off at higher odds than it appears to warrant, based on its past performances.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *úp Proto-Indo-European *-er Proto-Indo-European *upér Proto-Germanic *uber Old English ofer- Middle English over- English over- English load English overload From over- + load.

s.def: To load excessively.
To provide too much power to a circuit.
To create different functions for the same name, to be used in different contexts.
To fail due to excessive load.
An excessive load.
ex: If this last verbal overload has proven anything, it is that Rocko's Modern Life played better than it reads.

s.def: An overloaded version of a function.
ex: Code an overload of the insertion operator for the Rectangle class.

s.def: The damage done, or the outage caused, by such a load.
An load of goods above the prescribed carrying weight of the vehicle.
ex: We did haul overloads sometimes[.]

ety: From over + loading.

s.def: A type of polymorphism, where different functions, operators or variables with the same name are invoked based on the data types of the parameters passed.
ex: I guess we need to adapt to even more overloadings, since symbolophobia is part of Ada culture.

s.def: The loading of a vehicle etc. with too heavy a weight.
ex: Operators can be fined for overloading of vehicles.

ety: Inherited from Middle English overloken. From Middle English overloken; equivalent to over- + look.

s.def: A vista or point that gives a view down toward something else.
To fail to notice; to look over and beyond (anything) without seeing it.
ex: These errors were overlooked by the proofreaders.
We are more apt to over-look in any subject, what is trivial, than what appears of considerable moment […]
The place had been already searched and emptied. In the bar I afterwards found some biscuits and sandwiches that had been overlooked.

s.def: To pretend not to have noticed (something, especially a mistake or flaw); to pass over (something) without censure or punishment.
ex: I’m not willing to overlook such bad behaviour.
“Mr. Elton’s manners are not perfect,” replied Emma; “but where there is a wish to please, one ought to overlook, and one does overlook a great deal.”
Indeed, I have been a complete ass, and I know it. Will you overlook it this once and forgive me, and let things go on as before?

s.def: To supervise, oversee; to watch over.
ex: to overlook a gang of laborers
to overlook one who is writing a letter
His sole child, my lord, and bequeathed to my overlooking.

s.def: To offer a view (of something) from a higher position.
ex: Our hotel room overlooks the lake.
[…] she saw a figure standing by the rail of the balcony that overlooked the backyard.

s.def: To look down upon from above or from a higher location.
ex: The hill overlooks the valley.
Off with his head, and set it on York gates; / So York may overlook the town of York.
"'Twas young Wilson and a fireman wi' a ladder," said Margaret's neighbour, a tall man who could overlook the crowd.

s.def: To observe or watch (someone or something) surreptitiously or secretly.
To inspect (something); to examine; to look over carefully or repeatedly.
To look upon with an evil eye; to bewitch by looking upon; to fascinate.

ety: From Middle English oferrlaferrd, orlard, our-lord, ouyr-lord, equivalent to over- + lord.

s.def: A ruler of other rulers.
ex: The various tribal chieftains met each spring to elect an overlord that would lead them in time of war.
The leader is the man who knows the way of the overlords but identifies with the life of the oppressed.

s.def: A feudal lord directly owed rent or personal service by a tenant of subinfeudated land, a tenant's liege lord.
Anyone with overarching power or authority in a given domain.
ex: The crusty old professor was overlord of the history department, and few dared to cross his will.
One thing is for certain, there is no stopping them; the ants will soon be here. And I, for one, welcome our new insect overlords.

s.def: To rule over; to domineer.
ex: Poor Johnny one-note sang out with gusto / And just overlorded the place

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *úp Proto-Indo-European *-er Proto-Indo-European *upér Proto-Germanic *uber Proto-West Germanic *obar Old English ofer Middle English over English over Proto-Indo-European *leyg-der. s.def: To a high degree; very.
ex: I'm not overly enthusiastic about meeting him.

s.def: Superficially.
Carelessly, without due attention.
With a sense of superiority, haughtily.
Superficial; not thorough; careless, negligent, inattentive.
ex: Hee prayeth but with an ouerly desire, and not from the deepe of his heart, that will not bend his endeauours withall to obtaine what he desireth:

s.def: Having a sense of superiority, haughty.
Excessive; too great.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *úp Proto-Indo-European *-er Proto-Indo-European *upér Proto-Germanic *uber Old English ofer- Middle English over- English over- Old French maistrebor. Latin magisterder. Old English mǣġester Middle English maister English master English overmaster From over- + master.

s.def: To overpower or overwhelm.
ex: Sir Jasper started from his chair, ashamed of the sick fancies that had, for the moment, overmastered him.

ety: From Middle English overmacchen, equivalent to over- + match.

s.def: To match more than intended.
ex: The regular expression overmatched, capturing the entire paragraph instead of the specific sentence.

s.def: To be more than equal to or a match for, to surpass; hence, to conquer, vanquish.
To marry (someone) to a superior.
ex: If a yeoman have one sole daughter, he must overmatch her, above her birth and calling, to a gentleman forsooth, because of her great portion […]

s.def: A match in which one opponent is greatly superior to the other.
ex: […] we can increase the velocity of that force, so as to make it an overmatch for its antagonist.

s.def: An opponent who is more than a match for another; one who cannot be defeated.
ex: For Memnon […] fought hand to hand with his overmatch, and met his boyish and most dolorous death beneath the walls of Troy.

ety: From Middle English overmuche, overmuchel, from Old English ofermiċel, ofermyċel (“overmuch, excessive”), equivalent to over- + much. Compare overmany and overmore. Doublet of overmickle. Cognate with Scots over-mekill (“overmuch, excessive”), Old Norse ofrmikill (“overmuch, excessive”), Icelandic ofmikill (“overmuch, excessive”).

s.def: Very much; too much; overly much.
ex: So that contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow.
He had much prudence, much conscientiousness, and there were occasions when these virtues were the cause of overmuch disquietude in him.
This seemed to me a more important priority in 1959 than overmuch argument about nuclear philosophical heresies of one kind or another.

s.def: Excessive.
Too much; overly much
ex: Some readers do not care overmuch for poetry.
"[…] Do you be humble, and tempt you the Big Man not overmuch. He is quick to anger."
yet what am i that such and such / mysteries very simple touch / me,whose heart-wholeness overmuch / Expects of your hair pale, / a terror musical?

s.def: An excessive amount; too much.
ex: They had felled too freely here; the sawmills had taken over-much, leaving next to no young wood.
If citizens hear overmuch of the bliss of others, it galls the secrecy of their hearts.

ety: Inherited from Middle English overnyght, from Old English ofer niht (“through the night, overnight”), equivalent to over + night. Verbal use (late 19th c.) may have been influenced by German übernachten (16th c.), though it could also have developed independently. Compare also Dutch overnachten (“to overnight”), Middle Low German ȫvernachten (“to overnight”), West Frisian oernachtsje (“to overnight”), Saterland Frisian uurnoachtje (“to overnight”).

s.def: During or throughout the night, especially during the evening or night just past.
ex: Let it run overnight and we'll check on it in the morning.
They delivered the package overnight.

s.def: In a very short (but unspecified) amount of time.
ex: The change seemed to happen overnight.
"You can't overnight turn everyone into an expert on everything. [...]."

s.def: Occurring between dusk and dawn.
ex: The overnight ferry docked at 10 a.m.
Her stepfather, Duane Childers, was also asleep after working an overnight shift, […]

s.def: Complete before the next morning.
ex: Don't expect overnight delivery.
Federal Express handled 225 million overnight and second-day packages, cornering a 50-percent share of the entire domestic overnight market[…].
I like cold overnight oats eaten straight from the fridge.

s.def: For which participants stay overnight.
ex: They sent their kids to overnight camp.
We went on an overnight ski trip.
Overnight visitation in the park is controlled by the National Park Service and limited by the availability of lodging and camping facilities.

s.def: To stay overnight; to spend the night.
To send something for delivery the next day.
ex: We can overnight you the documents for signature.

s.def: An item delivered or completed overnight.
ex: Have you looked at the overnights yet?

s.def: Viewership ratings for a television show that are published the morning after it is broadcast, and may be revised later on.
ex: Word spread that Barney was on his way out to the location and that the Nielsen overnights had been terrific, or why else would he come.

s.def: The fore part of the previous night; yesterday evening.
ex: Pardon me, madam: If I had given you this at overnight, She might have been o'erta'en

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *úp Proto-Indo-European *-er Proto-Indo-European *upér Proto-Germanic *uber Old English ofer- Middle English over- English over- Proto-Indo-European *peth₂-der. s.def: A section of a road or path that crosses over an obstacle, especially another road, railway, etc.
ex: The homeless man had built a little shelter, complete with cook-stove, beneath a concrete overpass.

s.def: To pass above something, as when flying or moving on a higher road.
ex: Gillian watched the overpassing shoppers on the second floor of the mall, as she relaxed in the bench on the ground floor.

s.def: To exceed, overstep, or transcend a limit, threshold, or goal.
ex: Marshall was really overpassing his authority when he ordered the security guards to fire their tasers at the trespassers.

s.def: To disregard, skip, or miss something.
ex: A youth, how all the beauties of the East / He slightly viewed and slightly overpassed.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *úp Proto-Indo-European *-er Proto-Indo-European *upér Proto-Germanic *uber Old English ofer- Middle English over- English over- English pay English overpay From over- + pay.

s.def: To be more than an ample reward for.

ety: From over- + persuade.

s.def: To win someone over through persuasion; to convince (someone) to do something against their own judgement or wishes.
ex: And I let him overpersuade me. He was right, really.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *úp Proto-Indo-European *-er Proto-Indo-European *upér Proto-Germanic *uber Old English ofer- Middle English over- English over- English play English overplay From over- + play.

s.def: To play (a song or record) too frequently, often to the point of causing weariness and annoyance.
ex: A lot of times I don't want to overplay songs that I really like, because I know that then I'll get sick of them and I don't want to get sick of them.

s.def: To overestimate one's strength in a game or event, which ultimately may end in a defeat.
ex: Jack won the last match of blackjack; Theo overplayed.

s.def: To accidentally hit (one's golf ball) beyond "the green".
ex: The first few shots went wonderfully, but Robin overplayed the last and lost.

ety: From over- + Anglo-Norman plus, Middle French plus.

s.def: That which remains beyond what is necessary or required; a surplus.
ex: Where some for an over-plus, or supererogation have added this necessaity, that they must necessarily accompany them, as well in death, as in life.

s.def: To subdue someone by superior force.

ex: Bright light overpowers the eyes.

s.def: To render imperceptible by means of greater strength, intensity, etc.
ex: The dish was OK, but the garlic slightly overpowered the herbs.

s.def: To make excessively powerful.
present participle and gerund of overpower

The process of something being overpowered.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *úp Proto-Indo-European *-er Proto-Indo-European *upér Proto-Germanic *uber Old English ofer- Middle English over- English over- English price English overprice From over- + price.

ex: “Stable inflation is an oxymoron because it means it’s not stable,” Shelton told CNN in a recent interview.

ety: From oxytocic, from Ancient Greek ὀξύς (oxús, “swift”) + τόκος (tókos, “childbirth”, from τίκτω (tíktō, “I give birth”)).

s.def: A hormone that stimulates contractions during labor, and then the production of milk; also plays a role in social bonding.

ety: From Middle English oystre, from Old English ostre, reinforced or superseded by Anglo-Norman oistre, which is from Old French oistre, uistre (compare modern French huître); both lines (Old English and Old French) from Latin ostrea, from Ancient Greek ὄστρεον (óstreon). Doublet of ostro (“a purple dye”).

s.def: mollusk — see also clam, mollusc, mussel
food from mollusc

Any of certain marine bivalve mollusks, especially those of the family Ostreidae (the true oysters), usually found adhering to rocks or other fixed objects in shallow water along the seacoasts, or in brackish water in the mouth of rivers.
ex: He was a bold man that first ate an oyster.

s.def: The delicate oyster-shaped morsel of dark meat contained in a small cavity of the bone on each side of the lower part of the back of a fowl.
ex: Cut remaining skin on back. Remove the oyster (choice dark meat in spoon-shaped bone on back) with the leg.

s.def: Any of the fungi in the genera Pleurotus, Hohenbuehelia, or other related genera.
A pale beige color tinted with grey or pink, like that of an oyster.
A person who keeps secrets.
ex: Hard and sharp as flint, from which no steel had ever struck out generous fire; secret, and self-contained, and solitary as an oyster.
I will not be a human oyster. No, I will lay my cards on the table, which is assuredly a thing that oysters do not do.

s.def: Something at one's disposal.

ex: Harvesting wild oyster mushrooms has always been a favorite fall gathering activity for me as a Michigan outdoorsman.

s.def: Any of several mushrooms of the genus Pleurotus cultivated for food.
A rich viscid sauce made from oysters and brine, used in Chinese cooking.

ety: From oyster + catcher.

s.def: Any of several black or pied coastal wading birds in the genus Haematopus that have a long red or orange bill and feed on shellfish.
A dark waxy mineral, found associated with petroleum in some sandstones, used to make polishes.

ety: From German Ozon, coined 1840 by Christian Friedrich Schönbein, from Ancient Greek ὄζον (ózon), neuter participle of ὄζω (ózō, “I smell”), in reference to its pungent odour. The “fresh air” sense is from an erroneous former belief that seaweed contains and releases ozone.

s.def: An allotrope of oxygen (symbol O₃) having three atoms in the molecule instead of the usual two; it is a toxic gas, generated from oxygen by electrical discharge.
ex: Lightning flashed again, the thunder came a second later. It rained harder. The smell of ozone was strong. You could feel the charge in the air.
Martin said that the National Park Service invested in “a state-of-the-art ozone nanobubbler filtration system” that is intended to keep algae out.

s.def: Fresh air, especially that breathed at the seaside and smelling of seaweed.
ex: To Ramsgate baths she sped, in quest / Of seaweed and ozone ; / For seaweed and ozone were best, / They said, to give her tone.
It's got the lot: fresh sea air, ozone, seaweed. You could cut the air with a knife.
